question: The restriction of lead shot ammunition under the REACH Regulation raises particular concerns for Cyprus. Steel shot is unsuitable for the majority of hunting weapons on the island, while the absence of laboratories increases adaptation costs. According to the European Chemicals Agency, bismuth and tungsten-based cartridge options cost four to five times those using lead.

In addition, rocky terrain raises questions about the safety of alternative shot, owing to the ricochet risk arising from steel options. What is more, alternatives are more likely to simply injure game, rather than resulting in immediate death. All this, together with the cost of adapting shooting ranges, means that the transition to the new provisions of the regulation results in a disproportionate burden.
In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has it assessed whether the use of alternative shot affects the welfare of game, in particular the risk of injury without immediate death, as well as the risk of ricochet on rocky terrain?
How have the climate and soil conditions of Cyprus been taken into account when assessing the risk of lead pollution in soil and groundwater?

What measures does the Commission intend to consider to limit compliance costs for hunters, shooting ranges and small ammunition manufacturers, in particular with regard to the certification of antique weapons and the adaptation of infrastructure?
